Welcome back to Bartending Basics! I don't expect this to be the Big Boss of all bartending tutorials, I just want to give you a fundamental heads up about a few things. This post will detail different types of Liquors and Liqueurs, and even give you something to look for, next time you're getting a drink made.

Part 3.0: Types of Liquor

Whiskey - Whiskey is a spirit, aged in wood, obtained from the distillation of a fermented mash of grain. Whiskey is produced in four countries: the United States, Canada, Scotland, and Ireland. The whiskeys produced in Canada, Ireland, and Scotland take on the name of their countries. Whiskeys produced in other countries, even though they may taste similar, cannot legally be called Canadian, Irish, or Scotch.

Brandy - Brandy is a potable spirit, distilled from a fermented mash of grapes or other fruit. Most brandy is distilled from wine. White wine, made from white grapes, is used most often. Wine that has recently finished its fermentation process makes the best brandy. An aged wine, even if it is of superior quality, won’t make a good brandy.

Gin - Gin is distilled from grain and receives its unique flavor and aroma from juniper berries and other botanicals.

Rum - Rum is an alcoholic distillate made from the fermented juice of sugarcane, sugarcane syrup, sugarcane molasses, or other sugarcane by-products. It is often flavored.

Tequila - Tequila is obtained from the distillation of the fermented juice (sap) of the mescal plant, called pulque. The Mescal plant is a species of The Agave plant.

Vodka - Like whiskey, vodka is distilled from a fermented mash of grain, but they’re different in how they’re distilled. Whiskey is distilled at a low proof to retain flavor. Vodka, however, is distilled at a high proof, 190 or above, and then processed even further to remove all flavor. Most American distillers filter their vodkas through activated charcoal. Also, whiskey is aged, and vodka is not. Few, but some vodkas are made from potatoes. Vodka is often flavored.

Part 3.5: Liqueurs & Cordials

Amaretto - An Imported Italian liqueur made from apricot stones, which produce an almond flavor.Great on the rocks, or in an Amaretto Sour.

Chambord - Black raspberry liqueur from France made with small black raspberries, other fruits, herbs and honey.

Cointreau Liqueur - Imported orange liqueur from France. Similar to orange curacao. Clear in color. Flavor of fresh orange peels with a slight hint of spice. Used prominently in Margaritas!

Frangelico - Hazelnut Liqueur imported from Italy. A mix of hazelnuts, berries, and herbs. Flavors of hazelnut and butter.

Grand Marnier - Made with cognac, essence of wild oranges and delicate syrup, the mixture is aged in oak casks prior to bottling. There are many ways to drink it, but, as you might have guessed, my favorite way is in a Margarita. The addition of Grand Marnier to a top shelf Margarita, is called a Cadillac Margarita.

Jagermeister - Imported liqueur from Germany. Intensely herbal, citrus nose. Great with Red Bull, also great with Root beer.

Kahlua Coffee Liqueur - America’s number one imported liqueur. Aromas of coffee beans. Flavors of coffee and semisweet chocolate. An excellent addition to your morning coffee? I wouldn’t know, I’m not awake for morning anyway, well, not on the right side of it anyway.

Baileys Irish Cream - Cream liqueur imported from Ireland. A blend of real cream and Irish whiskey. Also great in coffee; but a prominent feature in the delicious Irish Car Bomb, which consists of a half shot of Baileys, and a half shot of Jameson, dropped into a half pint of Guinness. These go down smooth.

Brown Creme De Cacao - Brown color. Rich cocoa flavor.

White Creme De Cacao - Clear color, taste the same as the Brown Crème De Cacao.

Green Creme De Menthe - Dark green color. Mint flavor.

White Creme De Menthe - Clear. Natural mint flavor.

Creme De Banana - American banana flavored liqueur. The ‘Creme’ means that this liqueur is sweeter than most liqueurs, not that it is blended with cream.

Peppermint Schnapps - Peppermint flavored liqueur. Schnapps is less sweet than a liqueur. Great to just sip, on the rocks.

Peach Schnapps - Peach flavored. Most schnapps are generally low in proof and contain a lower sugar content than other cordials. A classic shooter, the Red Headed Slut, includes this, jagermeister, and cranberry juice.

Root Beer Schnapps - Root Beer flavored schnapps made in the U.S.

Buttershots Schnapps - Cordial that has intense butterscotch aromas and flavors.

Blue Curacao - Orange flavored. Made from orange peel. Blue color. Used for a variety of drinks, but my favorite is the Adios Mother Fucker. Which essentially a Long Island Iced Tea, but instead of Coke, you add Blue Curacao, and Sprite. A Long Island Iced Tea consists of Vodka, Gin, Rum, Tequila, Triple Sec (Or Cointreau.) Sweet & Sour Mix, or fresh sour mix if your bar is especially handy.

Triple Sec - Orange flavored liqueur. Orange peels are used for the flavoring. Similar to curacao, but more refined. A slightly lower quality liqueur than it’s companion, Cointreau. It’s used prominently in Long Island Iced Tea’s, and Margaritas.

Southern Comfort - A blend of bourbon and peach liqueur. Made from bourbon and peach liqueur in which fresh peaches were marinated. Often just consumed by itself, or with a mixer; but also included in a variety of mixed drinks.

Fireball - is a cinnamon-flavored whisky-based liqueur. Its foundation is Canadian Whisky, and the taste otherwise resembles the candy with the similar name. Mixes surprisingly well with Sprite, Dr. Pepper, and Root beer. Though, I enjoy Angry Balls now and again - A shot of Fireball mixed in with hard apple-cider - typically Angry Orchard.

Guys, this list doesn’t contain every single cordial, liqueur, or even liquor variation. It does, however, contain what would be included in what I would consider a pretty basic bar set-up. For the liqueurs, I’ve included pictures as a point of reference, so, that next time you’re at the bar, you can know what your bartender is using, as these liqueurs are often used in popular mixed beverages.
Bartending Basics Series: Part 3 Liquors & Liqueurs

As somebody new to achohol as a hobby, what's the real difference between a "liquor" and a "liqueur"? Obviously the latter tend to include more flavourful ingredients, but is there a real distinguishing feature? Are they a subset of liquors?

I don't really know much about this topic, but a simple Google search seems to have answered the question nicely --> http://grammarist.com/spelling/liquor-vs-liqueur/

It seems that the main difference is how the type of drink is prepared: a liquor is mainly the process of distilling something while a liqueur is the flavoring of a liquor. Again, not really knowledgeable in this area but hopefully this helps.

To say they are a subset of liquors would be too simple a definition. There are clearly similarities, though. Nowadays everything is 'flavored,' like this or that - but the real distinction between a liquor and liqueur is this: A liquor is an alcoholic beverage made of grains or other plants which is fermented into a potent Alcohol. A liqueur is a sweetened spirit flavored with various flavors, oils, and extracts. While a liquor can in fact be flavored, they tend still not to be as sweet as liqueurs.

They're US terms. A liquor is a distilled alchohol, usually not significantly sweetened or diluted and with savoury flavorings, if flavored at all. A liquer/cordial is distilled alcohol mixed with simple syrup (water + invert sugar) and flavoured with fruits/spices etc,

In Europe liquors are called "spirits," liquers are usually called liquors and "cordial" refers to a squash (flavoured concentrated syrup).

Rum - Rum is an alcoholic distillate made from the fermented juice of sugarcane, sugarcane syrup, sugarcane molasses, or other sugarcane by-products.

As far as I am aware it is not, while there is not D.O.G for rum, it is always made from sugarcane by products like molasses. Cachaca and Rhum Agricole are made from sugar cane juice. In countries where sugarcane industry has become redundant due to the sugar beet production in Europe and Corn syrup alternative state side, like Brazil or many french pacific Islands, they have converted the sugarplantations to distilleries and started making a spirit from the sugarcane juice as a default. This is still a **relatively ** new practice in terms of traditional rum production.

Tequila - Tequila is obtained from the distillation of the fermented juice (sap) of the mescal plant, called pulque. The Mescal plant is a species of The Agave plant.

Tequila comes from fermented pulque yes, but the pulque for tequila must be from the blue agave family or "agave azul" not agave mescal. Pulque is not so much a juice rather than a sap derived from cooking the Agave plants' heart or "stem" and mashing it. (it also has to come form the Jalisco Region and mixto can contain 50% other ingredients than agave).

Vodka - Like whiskey, vodka is distilled from a fermented mash of grain, but they’re different in how they’re distilled. Whiskey is distilled at a low proof to retain flavour. Vodka, however, is distilled at a high proof, 190 or above, and then processed even further to remove all flavor. Most American distillers filter their vodkas through activated charcoal. Also, whiskey is aged, and vodka is not. Few, but some vodkas are made from potatoes. Vodka is often flavoured.

Vodka can actually be made from any raw material not just grain, in fact i believe Smirnoff for your US market is made in the Caribbean from... sugarcane. (This with Smirnoff was 8 years ago before EU regulation came about as well, so I might be wrong by now) In Europe, there isn't such a focus on the distillation strength as there is in the US, but EU law specifically states that it should retain the characteristics of the raw spirit.- so the removal of all flavour is something specific to US vodka. (skyy etc). LINK to EU LAW btw

AmarettoPNG - An Imported Italian liqueur made from apricot stones, which produce an almond flavor.Great on the rocks, or in an Amaretto Sour.

I know few people who realise that Disaronno is flavoured with Apricot stones and not almonds, however there are Amaretto's that are flavoured with the real thing.

Cointreau LiqueurPNG - Imported orange liqueur from France. Similar to orange curacao. Clear in color. Flavor of fresh orange peels with a slight hint of spice. Used prominently in Margaritas!

Just for interest sakes, Cointreau is a triple sec, Cointreau is the brand, in fact their old labels used to reference it, the flavour is distilled into the liqueur which made it dry or "sec" back in the day. Today it is just sweet.

Similarly Grand Marnier is an Orange Curacao and used to be branded Curacao Marnier Curacao a liqueur traditionally made from dry Curacao orange peels soaked in brandy, and is supposed to be much sweeter. I doubt that the brand is still made with Cognac today but it used to be.

Southern ComfortPNG - A blend of bourbon and peach liqueur. Made from bourbon and peach liqueur in which fresh peaches were marinated. Often just consumed by itself, or with a mixer; but also included in a variety of mixed drinks.

Southern comfort has its origin in Whiskey, peaches, sugar and spice but the brand has not seen a drop of Bourbon or any whiskey for years. In fact they use peach flavour, whiskey flavour and a neutral spirit like vodka.

When I was twelve I was fooling about on a slippery dip with class mates. We were sliding down standing up, kind of pretending to skate down the dip. I fractured a vertebrae and did all kinds of damage to my spine, I can still walk, but it took years of steel braces and eventually years of yoga to really turn my life back around, but that's not my point.

My point is that when I was in chronic pain and unable to walk properly I couldn't do Physical Education at school, so I sat in a classroom by myself spent my time drawing. Ninja Turtles, Garfield and all kinds of Looney Tunes characters. I would also listen to music... and learn to enjoy my own company.

These days (more than twenty years later) I spend most of my waking hours making art and music and I just don't see how that would have happened without this ill-fated fall. It unknowingly pushed me towards art and music and ultimately afforded me the time to focus on such endeavours. It's weird, as much as living with chronic pain is a pain in the literal arse, I'm also strangely glad that my life offered me this awesome opportunity.

TL;DR - Suffered spinal injury, became artist.

When I was in third grade I was diagnosed with Aplastic anemia. Long story short, I ended up being very lucky and we beat the crazy odds and had my sister be an exact bone marrow match. I then underwent a bone marrow transplant and well I'm still here talking to you all, so things worked out well.

I feel like it had an impact on how I view the world. I'm no different than anyone else and get upset at the normal things in life that everyone does. I just try to always remember that life is too short and to just always try to enjoy yourself as much as you can. I also learned that no matter how bad you think that you have it, there are people out there that are way worse off than you. When I was at Boston Children's Hospital I was on a floor for kids that had cancers and leukemia, etc. During my stay there there were about 15 or so other children, of those I'm one of two that are still alive.

I feel very thankful that this all happened to me when I was so young. I felt that it made me more resilient even if it was because I was more ignorant of what was going on. I remember being told that I could die and everyone being so worried for me and just thinking, I'm not going to die. If I had to go through that same ordeal today with an adult understanding, it would be a totally different story.

Just a quick side story if anyone is still reading. An example of how things can always be worse was a boy that I remember meeting while at the Ronald McDonald House. He was older than me in his early teens and had a brain tumor. I remember that when they would walk down the street to the hospital it would be the boy and his mother and then his father 20 or so feet behind them. His father didn't want to walk with his son and his wife because he was ashamed that his son had a brain tumor. That always made me feel sad for him, since we had so much support from our family. Sadly I don't recall his outcome, I believe he survived but I'm not 100% sure. Either way I think about him every now and then and wonder how things may be going for him.

Was playing a friendly game of soccer with some friends, mini-field, small goals, nobody going very hard. One guy accidentally stepped on my foot, but it didn't really hurt, just felt a little bruised later on. It cleared up in a week and a month later I was running and all that. Woke up one Sunday morning, maybe 6 weeks after the incident, and my whole foot and lower leg was massively swollen and incredibly painful. I could barely walk on it and even then I had an extreme limp. Went to the hospital and they did x-rays and stuff, all of which came back negative. There was no bruising or discoloration. The doctor said it was just tendinitis, but that's obviously stupid because what would even cause that? And throughout my whole lower leg? It gradually went down in swelling over the course of over a year and for that entire time I had a limp. It eventually reached a manageable level of swelling that I could get used to and walk normally, and even run on it a bit. Four years and 6 doctors later I finally got an accurate diagnosis: Morton's Neuroma, the most common foot problem out there. But the doctor who diagnosed it didn't want to operate on it, even though it's a very simple procedure that has a quick recovery time. He said the nerve damage is "too diffuse", so he might not be able to find it. So I'm just going to have to live with a foot that is permanently swollen for the rest of my life.

tl;dr: Got my foot stepped on, now it's swollen forever.
